parole.significato: a type of large, boiled, Italian sausage

parole.significato: bruschetta (Italian bread topped with garlic and tomatoes)

Borrowed from Italian broccoli, plural of broccolo, from brocco (“shoot, sprout”).

parole.significato: compass (device used to determine the cardinal directions)
parole.testo: From Italian bùssola (compare French boussole), from Vulgar Latin *buxula, a diminutive form of Late Latin buxis (“box”), from Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís, “boxwood box, box”), from πύξος (púxos, “boxwood”). Apparently influenced by Spanish bruja (“witch”).
Derived from Italian bagaglio (“baggage”). Term literally means baggage in Spanish as well however has also become a shortening of bugayo de porquería, meaning piece of ass.

parole.significato: Cagliaritan (of, from or relating to the city and province of Cagliari, Sardinia, Italy)

parole.significato: caricature (pictorial representation of someone for comic effect)

Borrowed from Italian carmelita, from Latin carmelītes.
Borrowed from Italian carrettella, a diminutive of carretta (“cart”). Doublet of carreta, carretilla.

Borrowed from Italian regge (“church doors”), from Late Latin (porta) rēgia (literally “kingly door”).
Borrowed from Italian ramolaccio, from Latin armoracia, from Gaulish *are more (“about/around the sea”). Compare German Meerrettich.
From rizo or from erizar. Perhaps partly an adaptation of Italian arricciare; compare also Portuguese riçar.
Borrowed from Italian rucola. Cognate with English arugula.
Borrowed from Italian salato. Doublet of salario.
Borrowed from Italian salciccia, variant of salsiccia, derived from Latin salsus (“salty”).
Borrowed from Italian saltimbanchi, plural of saltimbanco.
Borrowed from Italian selvatico, from Latin silvāticus. Doublet of salvaje. More at selva.
Borrowed from Italian serenata, from the adjective sereno (“clear, calm”), from Latin serēnus (“calm”).
Likely derived from Italian segnarsi (“to subscribe”) which involves paying in advance.

parole.significato: sobrassada (spiced, cured pork sausage from the Balearic Islands)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian soprassata, perhaps via Catalan sobrassada.

parole.testo: 16th-century borrowing from Italian soda. Doublet of sosa acquired earlier from Catalan. Meanings of a beverage are semantic loan from English soda.
Borrowed from Italian soffitto, from Vulgar Latin *suffīctus, perfect passive participle of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten or fix onto”); compare Classical suffīxus.

parole.significato: an angry or discontented snort or grunt
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian soffione, from Italian soffiare (“to blow”)

Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superanus, from Latin super. Doublet of soberano.
Borrowed from Italian sorbetto, from Turkish şerbet (“sherbet”), from Arabic شُرْبَة (šurba, “a drink”), from Arabic شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”).
Probably a borrowing from Italian sordina.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian sottana (“cassock”), from Italian sotto (“below, under”), from subtus (“below, beneath”), from sub (“under”). See English soutane.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: peg (a short, thick piece of wood, metal, or other material)
parole.testo: Uncertain, probably borrowed from Italian tacco; ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *takkō (“twig, branch, shoot”).
Borrowed from Italian taffetà, from Persian تافته (tâfte, “tissue”).
Probably borrowed from Italian tagliare, from Late Latin taliāre. Doublet of tajar, which was inherited from Latin. Compare English tally.

parole.significato: any of various kinds of flat noodles, such as tagliatelle and taglierini
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian tagliarino or Piedmontese tajarin, respectively from tagliare, tajé (“to cut”). Equivalent to tallar + -ín.
Borrowed from Italian tempo. Doublet of tiempo.
Borrowed from Italian terremoto or Latin terraemōtus.
Pseudo-Italianism, derived from the Italian phrase testa di ferro (“iron head”). Compare Asturian testaferru, Leonese testaferre, and Portuguese testa de ferro.
Borrowed from Italian toca, tocca (“veil, silkcloth”), from Lombard toh (“headscarf”), from Lombardic *tuoh, from Proto-West Germanic *dōk (“cloth”). Compare French toque, of similar origin.
Borrowed from Italian torso, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”). Doublet of tirso and possibly trozo.

parole.significato: short in stature (said of a person)

parole.testo: Obsolete present participle of traficar (“to smuggle”), from Italian trafficare.
Borrowed from Italian trampolino, of Germanic origin.
Borrowed from Italian strapuntino, influenced by transportar.
Borrowed from Italian traffico (“traffic”), from Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcāre (“to rub across”). Doublet of tráfico, a borrowing.

parole.significato: trio, threesome (a group of three, especially for performance art)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent, dülbent), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband). Doublet of tulipán.
From Italian tombolo (“pillow”), from Latin tumulus (“mound”), from tumeō (“to swell”).

parole.significato: Used to show anger, displeasure, exasperation, repulsion, or negative reaction to something.

parole.testo: From urbano + -ístico, from urbanismo, form influenced or borrowed from Italian urbanistico.
Borrowed from Italian valigia, from Late Latin valisia.
Unadapted borrowing from Italian vendetta (“revenge”), from Latin vindicta. Doublet of vindicta, borrowed from Latin.
Borrowed from Italian vespa. Doublet of avispa.
Either from Italian violone or directly from viola + -ón.

parole.significato: virtuoso (exhibiting the ability of a virtuoso)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian virtuoso, from Latin virtuōsus (“virtuous”).
Borrowed from Italian vulcano from Latin Vulcanus (“Vulcan”), from Etruscan [script needed] (Velchans).
Borrowed from Italian via ferrata (literally “iron road”).
Borrowed from Italian alle vongole (“with clams”).

parole.significato: to wander, to ramble; to gallivant (to walk without a purpose or destination)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian girare via Lunfardo. Doublet of girar.
Borrowed from Italian zucchini, plural of zucchino, from zucchina.
Borrowed from Italian opera, from Latin opera (“work, labor”). Doublet of obra and huebra.
Uncertain. Likely either derived from Italian murare or French amurer.
Presumably from the same source as bizarre, which may be Basque bizardun (“bearded”), from bizar (“beard”), or from Italian bizzarro, further etymology unknown. See English bizarre for more.

parole.testo: From Old Spanish briza, thence of uncertain origin. Probably from Old French bise, bize, or from Vulgar Latin *bize, in which case likely of Germanic origin. Probably from Middle French colonel, from Italian colonnello, or alternatively from Old Occitan coronel, from a diminutive of Latin columna, becoming influenced by corona.

parole.testo: From dialectal Italian cucuruccio (“conical hood, cone”), from an intermediate Vulgar Latin *cuculullius (“cone, cowl”), from Latin cucullus (“hood, cowl, conical wrapper”). Shared origin with English cowl. An ultimate Celtic origin, either borrowed from, into, or influencing the Vulgar Latin form i

Borrowed from Latin lapis (“stone”), whence also English lapidary and lapis lazuli). Alternatively through Italian lapis; compare Portuguese lápis. Doublet of lápida.
